title: Orienting Response
subtitle: Automatic attention to novel or changing stimulation
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating orienting response across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain orienting response in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in orienting response.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to orienting response.

sections.explainSimply: The orienting response briefly shifts attention toward a new stimulus and may be followed by settling when no danger appears.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Some EMDR models propose repeated orienting plus safety contributes to reduced arousal, though evidence is less developed than working-memory accounts.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Orienting, habituation and parasympathetic changes are plausible contributors but not uniquely specific to EMDR.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of orienting response as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need orienting response to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not equate physiological settling with complete processing.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use orienting response to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses orienting response to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not equate physiological settling with complete processing. Evidence classification: theoretical and mixed evidence.
